title: Multi-Module Project Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of multi-module project design using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates multi-module project design.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Multi-Module Project Design** as part of **Packages, Modules, Dependencies, and Build Tools**. Build reproducibility depends on the Gradle Wrapper, compatible plugin/toolchain versions, declared dependency scopes, and repeatable test/build commands. Use the subtopics—Gradle Subprojects, Shared Libraries and Module APIs, Dependency Direction and Build Performance—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Real projects depend on reliable error handling, modular organization, reproducible builds, and safe language boundaries. This lesson helps turn isolated syntax into maintainable applications.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Build reproducibility depends on the Gradle Wrapper, compatible plugin/toolchain versions, declared dependency scopes, and repeatable test/build commands.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with gradle subprojects. Then compare it with shared libraries and module apis. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Gradle Subprojects
items.text: Gradle Subprojects is part of reproducible project configuration. Declare the dependency or plugin where it belongs, preserve a compatible version set, and use the Gradle Wrapper for repeatable builds.

items.title: Shared Libraries and Module APIs
items.text: Shared Libraries and Module APIs crosses a system boundary. Model success and failure, validate external data, apply timeout/retry rules deliberately, and keep credentials and database access out of presentation code.

items.title: Dependency Direction and Build Performance
items.text: Dependency Direction and Build Performance should be evaluated against input size, allocation behavior, and workload. Start with a correctness test and reproducible measurement; choose the simplest implementation that meets the requirement.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a Kotlin/JVM console project and run the configured Gradle application task, or use the Kotlin Playground for examples that need no external dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Multi-Module Project Design removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.
